models.name: Claude Sonnet
models.quote: My default model was usually Claude Sonnet, for some of the planning and analysis tasks I used Claude Opus, and for implementation tasks I frequently used Cursor's composer-2 model.

also.quote: Model: I used Sonnet 4.6 to generate the solutions.

models.name: Claude Opus 4.8
models.quote: Opus 4.8 compared the quality of both solutions and their tests, without knowledge of how the solutions were created.

history.quote: Here are some highlights from the results (model used was Claude Opus 4.7, same as for the coupling analysis):

review_style.value: Risk triage: probability, impact and detectability set how much she reads; sensors point her to where
review_style.quote: So, harnesses for me are all about improving how as a human I can prioritize where to put my review.

also.quote: Reflecting on these 3 dimensions helps me decide if I should reach for AI or not, if I should review the code or not, and at what level of detail I do that review.
Low probability + low impact + high detectability Vibe coding is fine! As long as things work and I achieve my goal, I don’t review the code at all.
Looking at the exceptions AI created (suppressed warnings, increased thresholds) was a good point to start my code review.
And the temptation to just check out and not understand the results anymore is a lot lower, I went back to reviewing results much more - and I mean that in a good way.

harness.value: Sensors sidecar running lint, types, tests, coverage and mutation testing next to the agent; weekly review skills
harness.quote: In all of the experiments described, I used a vibe-coded little “sidecar” application that could run all of my computational sensors.

also.quote: And I just go in there and I currently manually just run those once a week and see if there’s anything new.

rules_files.value: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md (identical): use uv, check the sensors
rules_files.quote: Use `sensors check .` regularly to get information about the code and test quality of your changes.

hooks.quote: GitLeaks runs as part of the pre-commit hook, I consider it to be a sensor as well, as it will give the agent feedback when it tries to commit (computational)

signature.caption: a sidecar the agent polls
signature.why: Our pick: she built a CLI that keeps linters, tests, coverage and mutation testing running beside the agent and hands it a short status with fix guidance, so it can self-correct before she reviews.
signature.quote: The CLI can offer both situational awareness for the human in supervised sessions, and a token-efficient and guidance-enriched summary to the agent.

archetype.why: Builds her own harness pieces: a sensors CLI, skills for it, an eval runner and a Pi extension.

signature_quote.value: I personally have stopped telling my coding agents to write tests first, let alone do TDD (which I never did, to be honest), until I see evals or other strong arguments that convince me otherwise.
